support.locus: Tabulae Iguvinae VIa 30-32 (Umbrian, in Buck 1904 text)
words: nerf arsmo ueiro pequo castruo fri salua seritu
śám naḥ bhava dvipáde śám cátuṣpade

cognate: Lat. pecua = Umbr. pequo = Ved. paśú- = Av. pasu- < *péḱu 'livestock'; Lat. salua seruassis = Umbr. salua seritu (Italic, *solh2-wo- + *ser-w-); the human member *wiHro- survives in Umbr. ueiro, Av. vīra-, Ved. vīrá- (RV 10.85.44 vīrasū́ḥ in the same śám-formula stanza).
drift_or_renewal: Latin renews *wiHro- 'men (of the household)' with pastores (herdsmen) while keeping pecua; Vedic recasts the merism descriptively as dvipád- / cátuṣpad- 'two-footed / four-footed' (RV 1.121.3d adds náryāya 'manly' to the two-footed member), with paśú- surfacing beside it in RV 3.62.14.
shared_syntax: Petition to a god for the safety/health of a two-member set, men + livestock, coordinated as a merism: Lat. pastores pecuaque salua seruassis duisque bonam salutem ualetudinemque (2nd sg. optative-subjunctive) ~ Umbr. ueiro pequo ... salua seritu (imperative) ~ Ved. śám ... dvipáde śám cátuṣpade (dative of benefit).
context: Cato's lustration prayer to Mars pater (Agr. 141) asks him to ward off disease (morbos uisos inuisosque ... prohibessis defendas auerrunces) and keep herdsmen and herds safe; the Iguvine prayer to Juppiter Grabovius asks the same for men and cattle; the Vedic formula asks a god (Rudra RV 1.114.1, Vāstoṣpati 7.54.1, Soma 9.69.7) for weal and freedom from sickness for the two-footed and four-footed. The slab Vedic anchor (RV 1.121.3d-4a) is not itself a petition (Indra props up heaven for the four-footed and the manly two-footed), so the congruent prayer context comes from the support; the slab pair attests the merism and the Italic wording.
phrase: *wiHro- *peḱu- (men and livestock) in a prayer for safety/health

words.etymon: pie-lex-pipleh1ti pípleh₁ti / pie-lex-piporti píporti / pie-lex-prneh3ti pr̥néh₃ti

cognate: Lat. pater = Ved. pitā́ (*ph2tḗr), used as title after a god's name in petition; Lat. Iu-piter (Cato 134 context line) is the univerbated vocative *dyew ph2ter = Ved. dyaùṣ pitar.
drift_or_renewal: The god-name slot is filled by different gods (Latin Mars, Janus; Atharvan Parjanya, Dyaus); the title *ph2tḗr is constant. In Latin the old Sky-god formula has become one word (Iuppiter), so a free pater title is added to other gods.
shared_syntax: Theonym + *ph2tḗr as address or predicate, followed by a petition for protection: Mars pater te precor quaesoque uti sies uolens propitius mihi ~ parjanyaḥ pitā sa u naḥ pipartu 'Parjanya (is) father, may he carry us across/protect us'.
context: Both are farmers' prayers for land and household: Cato's lustration of the fundus and Janus/Jupiter offerings; AVŚ 12.1 is the hymn to Earth (mātā bhūmiḥ putro ahaṃ pṛthivyāḥ), where the rain-god is named father beside Mother Earth.

support.locus: Pindar O. 7 (Οὐρανὸς ... καὶ Γαῖα μάτηρ); Hesiod Op. ~563 (γῆ πάντων μήτηρ); Aesch. Sept. 16 (Γῇ τε μητρί)

cognate: pitā́ = Pater, mātā́ = Mater (*ph2tḗr, *méh2tēr) as the paired titles of Sky and Earth; Ved. dyaúḥ = Lat. Iu- (Iuppiter) = Gk Ζεύς.
drift_or_renewal: Latin renews the Sky member (aether, a Greek loan, or caelum) and the Earth member (terra, not cognate with pṛthivī) but keeps both kinship titles; Greek keeps Γαῖα/Γῆ μήτηρ and pairs it with Οὐρανός or Ζεὺς πατήρ.
shared_syntax: Two-member pairing of Sky + *ph2tḗr and Earth + *méh2tēr, as parents of life: dyauḥ pitā pṛthivī mātā ~ Pater aether ... Matris terrai / ille idem Pater ... Mater ... terra.
context: av:AVŚ, 3, 23.s14 names Dyaus father and Pṛthivī mother of the plants (vīrudhām); Lucretius 1.250-251 and 2.991-998 have rain from Father Sky received by Mother Earth, who bears crops and plants. The slab's Latin anchor (Lucr. 2.610, within the Magna Mater passage that begins at 2.598 and identifies the Mother with the earth) carries only the Mother half; the Father half is in the support. Lucretius here partly follows Greek models (Euripides), so the Latin witness may be indirect; the Vedic-Greek pair is the firmer part.

words: ἀρνειὸν ταῦρόν τε συῶν τ' ἐπιβήτορα κάπρον

cognate: Lat. sus = Gk ὗς (συῶν) (*suH-), Lat. ouis = Gk ὄις/οἶς (*h2ówis), Lat. taurus = Gk ταῦρος; Xenophon has βοῦς (*gʷṓws) for the bovine member.
drift_or_renewal: Xenophon's prose list renews/expands the triad (βοῦς for ταῦρος, adds goats); Homer renews the sheep with ἀρνειός 'ram' but keeps ταῦρος and ὗς; Latin fuses sus-ouis-taurus into the compound suouetaurilia.
shared_syntax: Coordinated list of the three domestic victims pig + sheep + bovine offered together to a major god.
context: Cato's suouetaurilia to Mars pater at the lustration of the estate; Odysseus' expiatory triple offering to Poseidon (ram, bull, boar); Jason ordering cattle, sheep, goats and pigs for the Pythian sacrifice. The slab Greek anchor is a historian's prose list and only loosely congruent; the Homeric triad in support is the real Greek counterpart of the Latin compound.
phrase: pig-sheep-bull sacrificial triad (sus ouis taurus ~ ὗς ὄις ταῦρος)

words: ἀπὸ γλώσσης μέλιτος γλυκίων ῥέεν αὐδή

cognate: Lat. mel = Gk μέλι (*mélit); Lat. dulcis = Gk γλυκύς/γλυκερός (*dl̥ku-/*dlewku-).
drift_or_renewal: none in Latin/Greek; Indo-Iranian uses *médʰu instead (slab AVŚ 3.30.3 madhumatīṃ vācaṃ 'honeyed speech', B-70865), with the same use for sweet speech.
shared_syntax: Epithet + noun 'sweet honey' (melle dulci ~ μέλιτι γλυκερῷ) and comparative with honey as standard (dulcior melle ~ μέλιτος γλυκίων); in both languages the figure is applied to speech/poetry (Lucr. 1.947 musaeo dulci contingere melle ~ Il. 1.249 Nestor's voice sweeter than honey).
context: The slab Greek anchor (Plato Ep. 13) has γλυκύς only with οἶνος beside μέλι, so it attests the pair of words, not the collocation; the Greek collocation is in the Homeric support. Honey is the obvious standard of sweetness in any language, so independent creation is quite possible.

words: ὄνομ' ... τὸ γὰρ θέτο πότνια μήτηρ

words.etymon: pie-lex-dhedheh1ti dʰédʰeh₁ti / pie-root-dheh1-do dʰeh₁- / pie-root-dheh1y-suckle dʰeh₁y-

drift_or_renewal: Greek renews the verb *dʰeh1- (Ved. dadhé; Homeric ὄνομα θέσθαι in support) with denominal ἐπονομάζω, and the 'fame' noun *ḱléwos (śrávas) with φήμη 'report, auspicious utterance'.
shared_syntax: A son receives/takes a name for the sake of renown: sūnúḥ śrávase nā́ma dadhé (dative of purpose) ~ ὑὸν ... φήμης ἕνεκα ἐπονομάζοντας (purpose ἕνεκα + gen.).
context: Weakly congruent: RV 1.103.4 is about Indra taking a name for fame as dragon-slayer; Plato's law has kinsmen name an adopted son 'begetter and hearth-holder' for the dead man's line for the sake of good report/omen. Shared are the son, the act of naming and the purpose 'for renown'; the inherited core is the name-giving collocation *h1nómn̥ dʰeh1- seen in the Homeric and Vedic support.
phrase: *suHnús ... *h1nómn̥ *dʰeh1- (for *ḱléwos): giving a son a name for renown

note: All 173 bundles read. Most bundles pair Plato Leges/Epistulae or Xenophon prose with Cato De agricultura or AV formulas through common roots and hold nothing inherited. Claims come mainly from Cato's prayers (Agr. 134, 141) and Atharvan/Rigvedic formulas; generic matches left out: door-shutting (*dʰwer- + *kleh2w-, B-81974, B-d2621), ordinal series, father/mother pairs, night/evening.
